body.heading: A car on a rope, balanced
paragraphs: Most lifts are traction lifts: the car hangs from steel cables that pass over a large wheel, called a sheave, at the top of the shaft. On the other end of the cables hangs a counterweight — a stack of heavy plates that balances the car plus roughly half of a full load.

Because the two sides nearly balance, the motor turning the sheave only has to lift the difference. A car full of people going up needs a push; the same car coming down may need braking more than power, as the heavier side tries to fall.

body.heading: Stopping exactly at the floor
paragraphs: The control system tracks the car's position continuously and slows it as it nears the chosen floor, creeping the last few centimetres so the floor of the car aligns with the landing. Only then do the doors — driven by a motor on the car — open, dragging the shaft doors with them.

If the power fails, spring-loaded brakes clamp the sheave automatically; the car does not need electricity to stay put. That fail-safe habit — brakes on unless power releases them — runs through all lift safety design.

body.heading: The brake that changed cities
paragraphs: In the 1850s Elisha Otis demonstrated a safety gear that transformed trust in lifts: if the cable breaks, spring-loaded teeth or rollers jam against the guide rails and grip the car. He proved it by having his own platform's rope cut at a New York exhibition in 1854.

Modern lifts add an overspeed governor: a spinning device that trips if the car descends too fast, triggering the safety gear. With several independent cables, each able to hold the car alone, a free-falling lift is essentially a problem the design has already solved.
